title: 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles
summary: Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.
subject: History
unit: Road to revolution and the Revolution
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

compellingQuestion.en: Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Por qué los combates pasaron de Boston a Nueva York, y luego a través de Nueva Jersey, en 1775–1776?

questions.task: Open the Massachusetts bookmark and click the Lexington and Concord diamond, then Boston. Note the dates, and the winner from the symbol color and legend. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

student.en: Open the Massachusetts bookmark. Click the diamond at Lexington and Concord. When was it fought? Use the legend to find out who won.
student.es: Abre el marcador Massachusetts. Haz clic en el rombo de Lexington y Concord. ¿Cuándo fue la batalla? Usa la leyenda para saber quién ganó.

fill.en: Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord: ________ miles
fill.es: Mide la distancia en línea recta de Boston a Concord: ________ millas

answer.text: Lexington and Concord, April 19, 1775, an American victory. The siege of Boston ran from April 19, 1775, to March 17, 1776. Boston to Concord is about 16 miles (26 km) in a straight line, so expect answers of 15–17 miles.

title.en: Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?
title.es: ¿Dónde se combatió en 1775 y dónde en 1776?

questions.task: Zoom out to see all 21 battles, from Quebec to South Carolina, and sort them into two lists by year. Which colonies saw fighting each year, and what changed?

student.en: Zoom out until you can see every diamond, from Quebec to South Carolina. Click each one and write its name under the year it was fought. Which colonies had battles in 1775? Which in 1776? What changed?
student.es: Aléjate hasta ver todos los rombos, desde Quebec hasta Carolina del Sur. Haz clic en cada uno y escribe su nombre bajo el año en que se combatió. ¿Qué colonias tuvieron batallas en 1775? ¿Y en 1776? ¿Qué cambió?

table.caption: Battles on the map by year and winner
rows: Lexington and Concord, Boston (siege) and Gloucester (Massachusetts); Fort Ticonderoga and Crown Point (New York); Great Bridge (Virginia)
Moores Creek Bridge (North Carolina); Sullivan's Island and Breach Inlet (South Carolina); Gwynn's Island (Virginia); Trenton (New Jersey)
Brooklyn, Valcour Island, Pell's Point, White Plains, Fort Washington (New York); Fort Lee, Mount Holly (New Jersey); Newport (Rhode Island)

answer.text: Fighting began around Boston, then spread along the coast. From August 1776 most battles were in New York and New Jersey.

questions.task: Turn on Key Port Cities (it sits inside the Revolutionary War Battlefields group) and zoom to New York City. Compare its harbor and rivers with Boston's. What could a navy do from New York?

student.en: In Map layers, turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (it's inside Revolutionary War Battlefields). Zoom in on New York City. Compare its harbor and rivers with Boston's. What could a navy do from New York?
student.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), activa Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (ciudades portuarias clave; está dentro de Revolutionary War Battlefields). Acércate a la ciudad de Nueva York. Compara su puerto y sus ríos con los de Boston. ¿Qué podía hacer una armada desde Nueva York?

answer.text: The American Battlefield Trust says the city's "central position in the American Colonies and its port made it vital to commerce and a key strategic location", and that British warships could "dominate the river waterways that cut through New York City." The British left Boston in March 1776 and won at Brooklyn on August 27. ([Battle of Brooklyn, American Battlefield Trust](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/revolutionary-war/battles/brooklyn))

questions.task: Zoom in near New York City until the numbered turning points show, and follow circles 4 and 5. Find Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton, and note who won each. Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton.

student.en: Zoom in on New York City until the numbered circles appear, then follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton. Who won each?
student.es: Acércate a la ciudad de Nueva York hasta que aparezcan los círculos numerados y sigue los círculos 4 y 5. Haz clic en los rombos de Fort Washington, Fort Lee y Trenton. ¿Quién ganó cada batalla?

fill.en: Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton: ________ miles
fill.es: Mide la distancia de la ciudad de Nueva York a Trenton: ________ millas

answer.text: Fort Washington (November 16) and Fort Lee (November 20) were British victories; Trenton (December 26) was an American victory. New York City to Trenton is about 52 miles (84 km) in a straight line.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a route drawn with Sketch, or bookmarks saved for a short talk.

student.en: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two places on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos lugares del mapa. Puedes escribir un párrafo, dibujar en el mapa o hacer ambas cosas.

beforeYouStart.en: British soldiers marched out of Boston to seize weapons that colonists had stored at Concord. The fighting that followed started the American Revolution. For the next two years, the British army and navy and the new Continental Army, led by George Washington, fought over the colonies' cities, rivers and harbors.
beforeYouStart.es: Soldados británicos salieron de Boston para apoderarse de las armas que los colonos habían guardado en Concord. Los combates que siguieron dieron inicio a la Revolución estadounidense. Durante los dos años siguientes, el ejército y la armada británicos y el nuevo Ejército Continental, dirigido por George Washington, lucharon por las ciudades, los ríos y los puertos de las colonias.

readingTheMap.en: Diamonds mark battles: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory. Each diamond is placed at the battle's usual location, but the fighting covered a wider area: gray shaded areas show the battlefield, and areas with diagonal stripes show the core, where the fighting was heaviest. Zoom in to see white numbered circles: five turning points, numbered in the order they happened.
readingTheMap.es: Los rombos marcan las batallas: azul si ganaron los estadounidenses, rojo si ganaron los británicos. Cada rombo está en el lugar donde se suele situar la batalla, pero los combates ocuparon un área mayor: las zonas grises muestran el campo de batalla y las zonas rayadas, el núcleo, donde la lucha fue más intensa. Acércate para ver círculos blancos numerados: cinco momentos decisivos, numerados en el orden en que ocurrieron.

reflection.en: What did the map show you about 1775–1776 that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
reflection.es: ¿Qué te mostró el mapa sobre 1775–1776 que quizá no habrías notado solo con la lectura?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: No preparation beyond checking the map opens on student devices. Students don't need accounts to explore it; saving their own copy needs a sign-in.

misconceptions.claim: The early war was fought in Massachusetts.
misconceptions.response: By the end of 1776 the map shows battles in seven colonies and in Quebec.

misconceptions.claim: The winner is the side that lost fewer soldiers.
misconceptions.response: Bunker Hill is shown as a British victory, yet its pop-up says the British had twice as many casualties as the Patriots.

misconceptions.claim: The Americans lost every battle in 1776.
misconceptions.response: The map shows American wins in the South that year, such as Moores Creek Bridge and Sullivan's Island, as well as Trenton.

standards.text: Explain the issues surrounding important events of the American Revolution, including declaring independence; fighting the battles of Lexington and Concord, Saratoga, and Yorktown; enduring the winter at Valley Forge; and signing the Treaty of Paris of 1783
Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
Examine the causes, course, and consequences of the American Revolution
Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past

keyFacts: Battles on the map, 1775: Lexington and Concord, Apr 19 (American); Siege of Boston, Apr 19, 1775 – Mar 17, 1776 (American); Fort Ticonderoga, May 10 (American); Crown Point, May 12 (American); Bunker Hill, Jun 17 (British); Gloucester, Aug 8–9 (American); Great Bridge, Dec 9 (American); Quebec, Dec 31 (British).

Battles on the map, 1776: Moores Creek Bridge, Feb 27 (American); Sullivan's Island, Jun 28 (American); Breach Inlet, Jun 28–29 (American); Gwynn's Island, Jul 8–10 (American); Brooklyn, Aug 27 (British); Valcour Island, Oct 11 (British); Pell's Point, Oct 18 (British); White Plains, Oct 28 (British); Fort Washington, Nov 16 (British); Fort Lee, Nov 20 (British); Newport, Dec 8–12 (British); Mount Holly, Dec 21–23 (British); Trenton, Dec 26 (American).
New York's "central position in the American Colonies and its port made it vital to commerce and a key strategic location" (American Battlefield Trust).
Boston to Concord: about 16 miles (26 km) in a straight line. New York City to Trenton: about 52 miles (84 km).
